llm.def: A large language model is an AI trained on massive amounts of text data that understands and generates human-like text. Examples are GPT, Claude, and Gemini. LLMs are the foundation of most AI chat and writing tools.

rag.def: RAG combines a language model with a search across your own documents. Instead of relying only on training data, the system retrieves relevant text passages and generates answers based on them — more accurate and with fewer fabricated facts.

prompt.def: A prompt is the input or instruction you give to an AI. The clearer and more specific your prompt, the better the result. Good prompting is the most important skill when working with AI tools.

token.def: A token is the smallest unit of text that a language model processes — typically a word fragment. AI API prices are charged per token. Rule of thumb: 1,000 tokens correspond to roughly 750 words.

halluzination.def: A hallucination is a fabricated but plausible-sounding statement made by an AI. You should always verify important facts. RAG and citations reduce this risk.

finetuning.def: Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model using your own example data to a specific task or style. It requires more effort than prompting, but delivers more consistent results for recurring specialized tasks.

embedding.def: An embedding converts text into a list of numbers that captures its meaning. Similar content is therefore positioned close together — the foundation for semantic search and RAG.

agent.def: An AI agent independently completes multi-step tasks: it plans, uses tools, and reacts to intermediate results. Instead of just answering, it takes action — for example by researching, retrieving data, and executing steps.

multimodal.def: Multimodal AI processes multiple types of input — text, image, audio — in the same model. For example, a tool can describe a photo or evaluate a graphic and text together.

open-source-llm.def: Open-source language models are freely available and can be self-hosted — relevant for data protection and DACH compliance, since data never leaves your own system. Examples: Mistral, Llama, DeepSeek.

vibecoding.def: Vibecoding refers to building software through natural language: you describe what you want, and the AI writes the code. Tools like Lovable, Bolt, or v0 generate entire apps without traditional programming.

tts.def: Text-to-Speech converts written text into naturally sounding speech. Modern TTS voices are hardly distinguishable from real human speech — used for voiceovers, podcasts, and audio content.

dsgvo-ki.def: When using AI in the DACH region, data protection is the biggest hurdle. Important considerations are EU data residency, data processing agreements, and — for US providers — standard contractual clauses. Self-hosted models bypass the transfer problem.

ai-act.def: The EU AI Act is the EU's AI law. Starting August 2, 2026, transparency obligations apply: AI-generated content must be labeled and users must be able to recognize when they are interacting with an AI.

context-window.def: The context window is the amount of text a model can process simultaneously — measured in tokens. Larger windows allow processing of long documents or entire code repositories in one go.

api.def: An API is an interface through which your software communicates directly with an AI model without using the web interface. API usage is typically billed per token and is the foundation for integrating AI into your own products and workflows.

chatbot.def: A chatbot is a program that responds in natural language. Modern chatbots are based on language models and are used for customer support, research, and text work. Under the EU AI Act, users must be able to recognize as of 2026 that they are talking to an AI.

open-source.def: Open-source AI refers to models and tools whose code is freely available. They can be self-hosted and customized — relevant for data protection, cost control, and independence from individual vendors.

text-to-image.def: Text-to-image models generate images from a text description. They are used for illustrations, concept art, and marketing materials. Quality and style depend heavily on the prompt.

text-to-video.def: Text-to-video models generate short video clips from text. The technology is developing rapidly, but is currently better suited for short sequences than for long, consistent films.

voice-cloning.def: Voice cloning creates an artificial voice that resembles a real person. It is useful for dubbing and synchronization, but legally sensitive: consent is mandatory, and such content must be labeled as of 2026.

transcription.def: Transcription converts spoken language into text. It is the foundation for meeting minutes, subtitles, and searchable audio archives. For DACH regions, quality with German audio and data protection are important.

vector-db.def: A vector database stores embeddings and finds semantically similar texts in a flash. It is the memory behind RAG systems and semantic search.

mcp.def: The Model Context Protocol is an open standard through which AI models access external tools and data sources. It simplifies connecting agents with real systems like files, APIs, and databases.

reasoning.def: Reasoning models take more time to "think" before answering and work through tasks step by step. They are stronger at logic, math, and complex problems, but are slower and more expensive than standard models.

guardrails.def: Guardrails are rules and filters that limit the behavior of an AI — for example to prevent harmful or off-topic output. Important for companies to use AI in a controlled and brand-compliant way.

no-code-ai.def: No-code and low-code tools let you build applications and automations with little or no programming. Combined with AI, you can describe what you want in natural language and working software is created.

workflow-automation.def: Workflow automation automatically chains tasks between apps — for example "new email → AI summarizes → add to spreadsheet". Tools like n8n or Make are the foundation for many AI-powered workflows.

open-weights.def: With open-weights models, the trained weights are freely available so you can operate the model yourself. This is not the same as fully open source, but gives significant control over data and costs.

agentic-workflow.def: An agentic workflow is a chain where an AI agent plans and executes multiple steps, uses tools, and reacts to results — rather than just answering a single question.
